zh.title: 小引 · 一部从定义推起的书
zh.deck: 先认识这部书的几何写法，再听定义与附释里那个说话的人。

sections.heading: 一本书
paragraphs: 斯宾诺莎是十七世纪住在荷兰的人。《伦理学》他生前没有印。一六七七年他去世，同一年，朋友们把他的遗稿印了出来，书名页上作者不署全名，只印了 B. D. S. 三个字母。同年还有一个荷兰文本。
书的全名是：按几何次序证明的伦理学，分为五部分。
五部分依次是：论神；论心灵的性质与起源；论情感的起源与性质；论人的奴役，即情感的力量；论理智的力量，即人的自由。

sections.heading: 几何的写法
paragraphs: 按几何次序，是照几何书那样写。先立定义；再立公则，就是不另立证明，拿来就用的那几条；然后一条一条立命题，每条命题后面跟着证明。由命题直接推出来的，叫绎理。全书的命题一共二百五十九条。
可这本书不全是这些。命题中间夹着附释，那是他停下来另外说的话。第三部分到第五部分，前面各有一篇序言；第一部分和第四部分，后面各有一篇附录。

sections.heading: 先认几个词
paragraphs: 有几个词往下处处要用，先说到不卡住为止。
第一部分的定义里有四个。实体，是在自身之内，凭它自身就能被设想的东西。样式，是在别的东西之内，要凭那个东西才能被设想的东西；他也管它叫实体的种种状态。属性，是理智从实体那里看出来，当作组成它本质的东西。神，是绝对无限的存在，是由无限多的属性组成的实体。
往下他证明：除了神，没有别的实体，也设想不出别的实体；凡是存在的，都在神之内。无限多的属性里，书里讲到的只有两样：思想和广延。人的身体是广延的一个样式；人的心灵，是这个身体的观念。
这个神不照着目的做事。第四部分的序言里他说：那个永恒无限的存在，我们称之为神，或者说自然，它存在出于哪一种必然，行动也出于那同一种必然。神或者说自然这个说法，全书出现四次，都在第四部分。
后三部分的路是这样走的。第三部分把人的情感当作自然里的事来推，原始的情感他只认三种：快乐，悲伤，欲望。第四部分讲人管不住自己的情感，他把这种无力叫作奴役。第五部分讲理智能拿情感怎么办，那是他说的自由。

sections.heading: 引的本子
paragraphs: 底稿引《伦理学》，据一个未注明所用印本的公开拉丁文本。网站版保留底稿的译述，并以 The Latin Library 的拉丁文转录复核，文末列出各篇对应的位置与链接；这份转录同样不当作新编的校勘本。英文另行重写，不借用现代译本的措辞。

sections.heading: 下面各篇
paragraphs: 下面各篇看的是这本书的样子：一本从定义推到底的书，作者在哪几处自己开口，开口说了些什么。
篇末另有旁注，把一个当代的框架放在他旁边，那个框架叫 SAE。旁注只是旁注，不是论证，跳过不读也不妨。

notes: 各篇以部分、命题、附释、序言或附录定位。网站所列 The Latin Library 是复核用的公开转录，不冒称它就是底稿原先未注明的网页。
五部分命题分别为36、49、59、73、42条，共259条。“神或者说自然”的四次按拉丁文不同格形式合计，不按一个固定字符串检索。

en.title: A Book That Begins with Definitions
en.deck: Before the propositions, a few words. Before the system, a way of speaking.

sections.heading: The book
paragraphs: Spinoza lived in the seventeenth-century Netherlands. He did not publish the Ethics during his lifetime. In 1677, the year he died, friends published his posthumous writings. The author’s name appeared on the title page as initials, B. D. S. A Dutch edition appeared that year as well.
The full title announces an Ethics demonstrated in geometrical order and divided into five parts.

The parts concern God; the nature and origin of the mind; the origin and nature of the emotions; human bondage, or the power of the emotions; and the power of the intellect, or human freedom. The book’s destination is already visible in that sequence, but it takes a long route to reach it.

sections.heading: Geometrical order
paragraphs: The arrangement resembles a geometry book. Definitions establish the terms. Axioms state what will be taken as given. Propositions follow, each with its demonstration. Corollaries spell out consequences. Across the five parts there are 259 propositions.

But that is not all the book contains. Between the formal steps come scholia: remarks in which the author stops to explain, anticipate a reader or argue at greater length. There are prefaces, too, and appendices to Parts I and IV. The voice of the book cannot be found in the propositions alone.

sections.heading: A few terms before we go further
paragraphs: We need only enough vocabulary to avoid stumbling at every line. In Part I, substance is what is in itself and conceived through itself. A mode is in something else and conceived through that other thing: a modification of substance. An attribute is what the intellect perceives as constituting the essence of substance. God is an absolutely infinite being, a substance of infinitely many attributes.

Spinoza goes on to argue that no substance other than God can exist or be conceived, and that whatever exists is in God. Of the infinitely many attributes, the discussion concerns thought and extension. A human body is a mode of extension; the human mind is the idea of that body.

This God does not act for the sake of an end. In the preface to Part IV, Spinoza says that the eternal and infinite being we call God, or Nature, acts by the same necessity by which it exists. Forms of that pairing—God or Nature—occur four times in Part IV.

The later parts turn toward our lives. Part III treats emotions as events within nature and identifies three primary affects: desire, joy and sadness. Part IV calls our inability to govern the affects bondage. Part V asks what understanding can do about them. That is the route toward the freedom named in its heading.

sections.heading: Texts and renderings
paragraphs: The Chinese manuscript works from a publicly available Latin transcription without an identified printed base edition. For publication, the passages are checked against The Latin Library’s Latin text, with the relevant part linked after each essay. That transcription, too, should not be mistaken for a newly established critical edition.

The English is written afresh for these readings. Passages from Spinoza are rendered for the argument at hand rather than copied from a modern translation. Exact wording can be checked against the linked Latin.

sections.heading: The readings that follow
paragraphs: These essays look at the shape of the book. In a work that proceeds from definitions through demonstrations, where does the author speak up again, and what does he do when he does?
An optional note places SAE beside the passage. It is a comparison, not a demonstration of one system by the other, and it can be skipped. The first task is to listen to this book on its own terms.

notes: References identify parts, propositions, scholia, prefaces or appendices. The Latin Library supplies an accessible comparison transcription, not a claim to have reconstructed the author’s original textual source.
The five parts contain 36, 49, 59, 73 and 42 propositions respectively. The phrase God or Nature is counted with its Latin case forms, not merely as one exact string.
